bugs.summary: Update handling of overflow in integer operations

comments.text:
Created attachment 3747
__builtin overflow checks in arithmetic.c

Following up from r-devel: https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-devel/2026-June/084615.html

The initial motivation here is that `R_integer_times`, as currently implemented, relies on Undefined Behavior (UB):

```
// stylized from arithmetic.c
int z = x * y;
if ((double)x * (double)y == z && z != NA_INTEGER)
  return z;
```

I.e., _after_ running the multiplication in `int`, we check if wraparound happened _in `double`_ (into which `int` embeds faithfully). The comment in the code acknowledges this is UB.

My initial proposal was to use `int64_t` instead, but Brian points out it is not universally available and indeed it's basically not used elsewhere in the R sources. The widely available `int_fast64_t` seems much more appropriate here than `int_least64_t`.

Luke also mentions `__builtin_mul_overflow` [1][2], which are recent enough (e.g. 2015) to necessitate some `configure` checks to activate, but which _are_ supported by `gcc` and `clang`.

On r-devel, I mentioned a quick benchmark in support of moving away from `double` -- now I've made that more formal by running the benchmark on GitHub Actions in the R mirror [3] by adding in `reg-tests-2.R` a snippet:

```
x <- y <- rep(10000L, 5e7)
print(system.time(for(i in 1:100) x * y))
```

And extracting the timings from 4 different proposals [4][5][6][7]. 

Here is the benchmark timings table (unit: seconds) compiled from the logs:

| Flavor | baseline | int64_t | int_fast64_t | \_\_builtin\_mul\_overflow |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Linux (clang, debian:stable, arm)** | 14.084 | 12.915 | 12.815* | 13.521 |
| **Linux (clang, debian:stable, intel)** | 15.528 | 10.573 | 10.694 | 10.379* |
| **Linux (clang, debian:testing, arm)** | 14.400 | 12.896 | 12.757* | 13.799 |
| **Linux (clang, debian:testing, intel)** | 15.487 | 10.776 | 10.612* | 10.639 |
| **Linux (gcc, debian:stable, arm)** | 14.940 | 12.588 | 12.518* | 14.285 |
| **Linux (gcc, debian:stable, intel)** | 13.983 | 10.046 | 9.318* | 9.441 |
| **Linux (gcc, debian:testing, arm)** | 14.731 | 12.707* | 12.870 | 14.386 |
| **Linux (gcc, debian:testing, intel)** | 14.753 | 11.719 | 10.903 | 8.704* |
| **MacOS (macOS-26)** | 8.977 | 10.001 | 8.855* | 11.006 |
| **MacOS (macOS-26-intel)** | 22.831 | 21.492 | 21.802 | 20.030* |
| **Windows (aarch64)** | 12.250 | 11.050 | 10.980* | 11.940 |
| **Windows (x86_64)** | 14.990 | 6.350* | 12.250 | 11.310 |

Note that these timings all have a fair amount of overhead from R -- I'm trying to make it a bit more realistic to show how the end user will perceive the change. This is of course far from comprehensive. Another way to view this is comparing the assembly output of the two approaches (`double` vs. `int_fast64_t`). Consider this minimized script:

```
// compare.c
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stddef.h>

#define R_INT_MAX  2147483647
#define R_INT_MIN -2147483647
#define NA_INTEGER -2147483648

#define GOODIPROD_DOUBLE(x, y, z) ((double) (x) * (double) (y) == (z))

int times_double(int x, int y, bool *pnaflag) {
    if (x == NA_INTEGER || y == NA_INTEGER) return NA_INTEGER;
    int z = x * y;
    if (GOODIPROD_DOUBLE(x, y, z) && z != NA_INTEGER)
	return z;
    else {
	if (pnaflag != NULL) *pnaflag = true;
	return NA_INTEGER;
    }
}

int times_fast64(int x, int y, bool *pnaflag) {
    if (x == NA_INTEGER || y == NA_INTEGER) return NA_INTEGER;
    int_fast64_t prod = (int_fast64_t)x * (int_fast64_t)y;
    if (prod >= R_INT_MIN && prod <= R_INT_MAX && prod != NA_INTEGER) {
        return (int)prod;
    } else {
        if (pnaflag != NULL) *pnaflag = true;
        return NA_INTEGER;
    }
}
```

In the generated assembly (`gcc -O2 -S -masm=intel compare.c -o compare.s`, and similarly for `clang`), I see:

```
times_double:
.LFB0:
        .cfi_startproc
        mov     r8, rdx
        cmp     edi, -2147483648
        je      .L2
        cmp     esi, -2147483648
        sete    cl
        je      .L2
        pxor    xmm0, xmm0
        pxor    xmm1, xmm1
        mov     eax, edi
        cvtsi2sd        xmm1, esi
        cvtsi2sd        xmm0, edi
        mulsd   xmm0, xmm1
        imul    eax, esi
        pxor    xmm1, xmm1
        cvtsi2sd        xmm1, eax
        ucomisd xmm0, xmm1
        setnp   dl
        cmovne  edx, ecx
        test    dl, dl
        je      .L5
        cmp     eax, -2147483648
        je      .L5
        ret
        .p2align 4,,10
        .p2align 3
```

Compared to:

```
times_fast64:
.LFB1:
        .cfi_startproc
        mov     rcx, rdx
        cmp     edi, -2147483648
        je      .L14
        cmp     esi, -2147483648
        je      .L14
        movsx   rdi, edi
        movsx   rsi, esi
        mov     edx, 4294967294
        imul    rdi, rsi
        lea     rax, 2147483647[rdi]
        cmp     rdx, rax
        jb      .L15
        mov     eax, edi
        ret
        .p2align 4,,10
        .p2align 3
```

`cvtsi2sd`, `mulsd`, and `ucomisd` are all relatively expensive compared to `movsx`, `imul`, and `cmp`.

So to me, this is really about whether we should use `int_fast64_t` or `__builtin_mul_overflow`. The appeal of the latter is that it is _designed_ explicitly for what we're trying to do. The code is also quite clean.

Lastly, while this started from improving integer _multiplication_ in this file, we might as well address the checks for overflow in _subtraction and addition_ while we're at it. The principle is the same -- we can refactor to either (1) explicitly embed in a 64-bit type, probably `int64_t` or (2) use `__builtin_{add,sub}_overflow`. It's not formalized yet, but a quick benchmark shows a similar conclusion -- we can do way better than the current implementation with either approach.

I think all of the approaches are pretty straightforward; I'm attaching a PoC patch of the `__builtin_{add,sub,mul}_overflow`.

[1] https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-13.3.0/gcc/Integer-Overflow-Builtins.html
[2] https://clang.llvm.org/docs/LanguageExtensions.html#checked-arithmetic-builtins
[3] https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/pull/272
[4] https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/actions/runs/28381932448 (baseline)
[5] https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/actions/runs/28414598687 (`int64_t`)
[6] https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/actions/runs/28421249004 (`int_fast64_t`)
[7] https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/actions/runs/28425139273 (`__builtin_mul_overflow`)
